paragraphs: This paper studies when gradient descent can successfully train a graph neural network. Its setting is realizable: the data comes from a network with unknown weights, and training aims to recover a solution with nearly optimal error. The central difficulty is that a graph network passes information between connected nodes, making its training dynamics harder to analyze than those of a standard feed-forward network.

The authors establish convergence results for two architectures. For deep linear graph networks, under assumptions on the data distribution, reaching error ε requires O(log(1/ε)) iterations. For graph networks with one round of message passing and ReLU activations, they prove a bound of O((1/ε²) log(1/ε)) iterations.

These results provide mathematical support for successful optimization in the specific settings analyzed. They also distinguish how the proven iteration requirements depend on the requested accuracy for the two architectures. The contribution is a step toward understanding graph-network training through its message-passing structure, with guarantees tied to the stated model and data conditions.
neurips-2021-a-convergence-analysis-of-g.tldr: The paper proves gradient-descent convergence rates for deep linear and one-round ReLU graph networks in a realizable setting.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning trains an agent from a fixed dataset. A central problem is that the agent can assign inaccurate values to actions poorly represented in that data. Many methods address this by restricting the learned policy toward recorded actions, but introduce extra models, tuning choices, and changes to the underlying learning algorithm.

This paper asks how much of that machinery is needed for strong performance. The proposed approach makes two changes to an existing online reinforcement-learning algorithm: it adds a behavior-cloning term to the policy update and normalizes the data. The cloning term encourages the policy to reproduce actions in the dataset while the reinforcement-learning update continues to guide improvement.

The authors report performance matching state-of-the-art offline methods while more than halving overall runtime by removing additional computational overhead. The finding makes a practical case for a baseline that is easy to implement and tune. It shows that, in the reported evaluation, a small intervention can address the offline setting effectively without a complicated collection of auxiliary components.
neurips-2021-a-minimalist-approach-to-of.tldr: Adding behavior cloning and data normalization to an online RL algorithm matches reported leading offline performance with less than half the runtime.

paragraphs: This paper investigates how neural responses from different animals can reveal a shared representation of stimuli. Finding that common structure matters both for understanding brain computation and for systems that use neural activity to identify inputs. The task combines aligning responses across animals with determining which stimulus produced the activity on an individual trial.

The authors propose a probabilistic method that maps stimulus-evoked responses into a shared low-dimensional representation. They then use hierarchical inference to decode the stimulus responsible for a trial. This connects the alignment and decoding tasks: the shared representation provides a common space in which responses from multiple animals can support stimulus identification.

The decoder is reported to withstand a range of neural-response characteristics and significantly outperform existing alignment procedures. Applied to mouse olfactory-bulb recordings, it reveals population dynamics that distinguish odors while retaining consistent structure across animals. These findings support the proposed use of shared neural representations to improve the robustness and scalability of chemical detection based on neural activity.
neurips-2021-across-animal-odor-decoding.tldr: A probabilistic alignment method finds shared odor-specific neural dynamics across mice and improves stimulus decoding.

paragraphs: Object detectors must place bounding boxes accurately around objects, and the training loss determines how errors in those boxes influence learning. A common choice uses intersection over union, or IoU, which measures the overlap between a predicted box and its target. This paper generalizes IoU-based losses into a family controlled by one power parameter, α.

The proposed α-IoU losses contain both a powered IoU term and a powered regularization term. The authors analyze whether the transformation preserves ordering and how it changes the weighting of losses and gradients. These properties help explain how modifying α can change the training signal while retaining a relationship to the original overlap-based objective.

Experiments across multiple detection models and benchmarks show that the losses can noticeably outperform existing IoU variants. Adjusting α gives detectors flexibility in reaching different levels of box accuracy. The authors also report improved robustness with small datasets and noisy bounding boxes. Together, these findings make loss design itself a useful way to influence localization accuracy and training behavior.
neurips-2021-alpha-iou-a-family-of-power.tldr: α-IoU introduces a single power parameter that adjusts bounding-box training losses and improves detection results in reported experiments.

paragraphs: Decentralized online learning lets multiple learners update models and exchange information as data arrives. When updates are synchronized, faster learners must wait for slower ones. This straggler problem can reduce the efficiency of the whole system. The paper studies an asynchronous alternative in which each learner proceeds at its own pace.

The authors first formalize asynchronous decentralized online convex optimization using an event-indexing system. This provides a way to describe updates and communications that do not share a single synchronized step. They then introduce AD-OGP, an algorithm combining asymmetric gossip communication with instantaneous model averaging to coordinate learning across the network.

The theoretical analysis bounds regret, a measure of accumulated learning performance, in terms of network structure and both processing and communication delays. This explicitly connects the learning guarantee to conditions in the distributed system. Experiments show that AD-OGP runs significantly faster than its synchronous counterpart and support the theoretical results. The contribution therefore combines a formal account of asynchronous learning with an algorithm that demonstrates practical speed benefits.
neurips-2021-asynchronous-decentralized-.tldr: AD-OGP enables decentralized learners to work asynchronously, with delay-dependent regret guarantees and reported speed gains over synchronous learning.

paragraphs: This paper addresses allocating coupons to improve customer retention while staying within a fixed budget. The decision space can be large because an e-commerce platform may serve many users and offer numerous coupon types. Business changes also require policies to adapt quickly, making repeated expensive training a practical obstacle.

A standard formulation uses a Lagrangian multiplier, λ, to express the budget trade-off. Existing approaches described in the abstract relearn their policy when λ changes. BCORLE(λ) instead introduces λ-generalization, allowing policy learning to adapt across multiplier values without starting from scratch each time. This targets the computational cost of responding to changing budget-related choices.

The framework also supplies an offline reinforcement-learning method for learning allocation policies and an off-policy evaluation algorithm for assessing them. Experiments in simulation and a real e-commerce market support its effectiveness. The authors report improved retention while keeping costs within budget, alongside reduced computation from reusing learning across λ values. The contribution connects budget adaptation, policy learning, and evaluation within one allocation framework.
neurips-2021-bcorle-lambda-an-offline-re.tldr: BCORLE(λ) learns and evaluates budget-constrained coupon policies that adapt across budget trade-offs without retraining from scratch.

paragraphs: Recovering a three-dimensional scene from an image requires finding scene properties whose rendered projection explains the observed pixels. Gradient-based optimization needs useful derivatives through the rendering process, but some rendering operations are not differentiable. Existing approaches often smooth these operations, and the particular approximation can affect the resulting scene estimate.

This paper studies differentiable rendering through randomized optimization and perturbed optimizers. It connects established renderer formulations to optimizers smoothed through randomness, then introduces differentiable perturbed renderers. The method also includes variance reduction to reduce the computational burden of perturbation-based estimation and an adaptive procedure that adjusts rendering smoothness automatically.

The authors apply the approach to 6D pose estimation and three-dimensional mesh reconstruction. They report more accurate solutions than state-of-the-art alternatives using smooth gradient approximations, attributing the benefit to informative gradients that guide reconstruction. The contribution is both conceptual and practical: it gives a broader optimization-based account of differentiable rendering and uses that account to improve the signals available for recovering a scene.
neurips-2021-differentiable-rendering-wi.tldr: Perturbed renderers use randomized optimization, variance reduction, and adaptive smoothing to improve reported pose and mesh reconstruction accuracy.

paragraphs: Differentiable programming makes it possible to train models by following gradients through their computations. Standard tools typically require differentiable model components, which limits their use with some piecewise-defined functions. This paper develops a principled way to extend gradient-based optimization to functions well represented by splines, a broad family built from polynomial pieces.

The key step is deriving a weak Jacobian, a generalized form of the derivative information needed to propagate changes through the model. The authors show that this Jacobian has a block-sparse structure. That structure allows it to be computed implicitly and efficiently, making the proposed derivative treatment usable as part of a predictive model.

The redesigned Jacobian is incorporated into a differentiable layer. The authors report improved performance in image segmentation, three-dimensional point-cloud reconstruction, and finite element analysis, and release their code. The significance is the connection between the mathematics of spline functions and a practical learning component: models can use spline-based structure while obtaining derivative information suitable for gradient-based optimization.
neurips-2021-differentiable-spline-appro.tldr: An efficiently computed weak Jacobian turns spline approximations into useful differentiable layers for several prediction and reconstruction tasks.

paragraphs: When several signals contain information about a target, their contributions can overlap, complement one another, or provide knowledge available from only one signal. Partial information decomposition separates these redundant, synergistic, and unique contributions. This paper develops a method for estimating unique information in general continuous distributions, focusing on one target variable and two source variables.

The method solves an optimization problem over distributions that preserve specified two-variable marginals. It combines copula decompositions, which describe dependence structure, with optimization techniques developed for variational autoencoders. This provides a computational route beyond the Gaussian and discrete settings that had received more attention.

The estimates agree closely with known analytical results for Gaussian distributions. In brain-inspired models, the method recovers effective connectivity in a chaotic network of rate neurons and reveals a complex trade-off among information components in recurrent networks trained on generalized XOR. These demonstrations show how the estimator can examine both network relationships and the way several signals jointly support a computation.
neurips-2021-estimating-the-unique-infor.tldr: The paper estimates unique information for continuous variables using copula-based optimization and demonstrates its usefulness in neural models.

paragraphs: Backdoor poisoning inserts mislabeled training examples carrying a watermark. A trained model can still perform normally on ordinary inputs while reliably making mistakes on inputs with that watermark. This paper builds a theoretical framework for analyzing such attacks in classification, covering both statistical vulnerability and the computational problem of defending against them.

The authors introduce memorization capacity as a parameter describing a learning problem's intrinsic susceptibility to backdoors. They use it to construct explicit attacks in vulnerable settings and establish that successful attacks are impossible in some natural problem settings. This separates circumstances in which the learning problem permits an attack from those in which it supports robustness.

Under certain assumptions, the paper also shows that adversarial training can detect backdoors. Under similar assumptions, identifying watermarked training examples and achieving robust generalization are nearly equivalent problems. The resulting necessity-and-sufficiency claim is asymptotic and conditional: within the analyzed setting, developing algorithms that filter poisoned examples is closely tied to learning models that generalize and resist backdoors.
neurips-2021-excess-capacity-and-backdoo.tldr: A theoretical framework links backdoor vulnerability to memorization capacity and conditionally connects robust learning with filtering poisoned examples.

paragraphs: A reward function should guide an agent toward desired behavior, but it can also shape how easily the agent learns and how understandable the rewards appear. This paper studies rewards with two properties: informativeness, intended to accelerate convergence, and sparseness, used as a proxy for interpretability. These goals can conflict because informative feedback often requires rewards at many points.

The proposed ExpRD framework treats reward design as a discrete optimization problem. It seeks a balance between those properties while guaranteeing that an optimal policy induced by the reward belongs to a specified target set. Its informativeness criterion evaluates how optimal or suboptimal target policies are across different time horizons and actions from each starting state.

The authors analyze the framework mathematically and relate it to existing techniques, including potential-based reward shaping. Experiments on two navigation tasks demonstrate its effectiveness at constructing explicable rewards. The contribution is a structured way to negotiate the trade-off between frequent learning guidance and sparse rewards while preserving the stated connection to target behavior.
neurips-2021-explicable-reward-design-fo.tldr: ExpRD balances informative and sparse rewards while ensuring that an induced optimal policy lies within a target policy set.

paragraphs: This paper studies reinforcement learning with an entropic risk measure, where the learning objective incorporates sensitivity to risk. Earlier work had established finite-time regret guarantees, but an exponential gap remained between upper and lower bounds. That gap left a substantial mismatch between proven algorithm performance and the limits expressed by the lower bounds.

The authors identify shortcomings in existing algorithms and their analysis, then transform the risk-sensitive Bellman equations into what they call an exponential Bellman equation. Bellman equations connect values across successive decisions. Recasting them provides a different basis for analyzing the backup operations that propagate those values through a learning algorithm.

The transformed equation also motivates a new exploration mechanism, linking the mathematical reformulation to how the agent gathers information. Together, the revised analysis and algorithmic changes yield improved regret upper bounds. The stated result tightens existing guarantees rather than claiming that the entire upper–lower bound gap disappears. Its main contribution is showing how a change in the value-equation formulation can support better risk-sensitive learning guarantees.
neurips-2021-exponential-bellman-equatio.tldr: An exponential transformation of risk-sensitive Bellman equations motivates new analysis and exploration that improve regret upper bounds.

paragraphs: Visual question answering asks a model to answer questions about an image. Although results on the widely used VQA v2 dataset were approaching human accuracy, interactions with leading models still exposed mistakes. This paper investigates that mismatch by building a benchmark around questions that people deliberately create to challenge a model.

Human participants interact with a state-of-the-art visual question-answering system. For each image, they try to find a question that causes it to predict an incorrect answer. The resulting AdVQA benchmark makes model failure part of the data-collection process, turning human attempts to expose weaknesses into a structured evaluation set.

A broad range of leading models performs poorly on the collected examples. This shows that strong performance on the commonly used benchmark can coexist with substantial vulnerability to human-designed questions. The authors also analyze the adversarial examples and offer guidance for future research. The benchmark's purpose is to make those weaknesses measurable and help direct progress toward image-question answering that withstands this more demanding form of evaluation.
neurips-2021-human-adversarial-visual-qu.tldr: AdVQA collects human-written questions that expose substantial weaknesses in leading visual question-answering models.

paragraphs: Domain generalization trains a predictor on related domains and evaluates it on a distinct domain it has never seen. This matters because strong performance on training-like data can coexist with severe failure under a distribution change. The paper develops an approach that explicitly connects generalization to a model of how data is generated.

Under that data-generation model and an associated invariance condition, the authors show that domain generalization is equivalent to an infinite-dimensional constrained learning problem. They then use nonconvex duality theory to derive unconstrained relaxations with tight bounds on the duality gap. These relaxations provide a more tractable foundation for the proposed learning algorithm, which has convergence guarantees.

Experiments report improvements of up to 30% over leading domain-generalization baselines across benchmarks including ColoredMNIST, Camelyon17-WILDS, FMoW-WILDS, and PACS. The theoretical equivalence depends on the stated modeling and invariance conditions, while the reported gains are empirical. Together, they connect a principled formulation of domain change with an algorithm that performs strongly in the evaluated settings.
neurips-2021-model-based-domain-generali.tldr: Model-Based Domain Generalization derives a convergent algorithm from a conditional constrained-learning formulation and reports benchmark improvements of up to 30%.

paragraphs: Bayesian optimization searches for good inputs to functions that are expensive to evaluate. This paper considers a complication: different inputs can cost different amounts to evaluate, those costs may be unknown, and the total search must respect a budget. Learning which evaluations are affordable therefore consumes some of the same resources needed to improve the objective.

The authors show that expected improvement and expected improvement per unit cost can be arbitrarily worse than an optimal policy that considers future decisions. This is a possibility result about their shortcomings, rather than a claim that they always perform poorly. It motivates an acquisition function that reasons beyond the immediate next evaluation.

The proposed budgeted multi-step expected improvement extends classical expected improvement to unknown, heterogeneous costs under a budget. Its forward-looking structure accounts for how a current evaluation affects later opportunities. Experiments on synthetic and real problems show it outperforming existing methods. The contribution is a way to make evaluation cost, uncertainty about that cost, and remaining search opportunities part of one decision rule.
neurips-2021-multi-step-budgeted-bayesia.tldr: Budgeted multi-step expected improvement plans Bayesian-optimization evaluations ahead while accounting for unknown costs and a total budget.

paragraphs: Importance sampling depends on proposal distributions that determine where samples are drawn. When sampling procedures are nested, the quality of proposals at multiple levels matters. This paper introduces nested variational inference, or NVI, a family of methods that learns those proposals through objectives attached to each level of the sampling procedure.

At each level, NVI minimizes either a forward or reverse KL divergence, a measure of discrepancy between distributions. The framework applies to many commonly used importance-sampling strategies and can also learn intermediate densities. These intermediate distributions act as guides, giving the sampler useful direction as it moves through a multi-stage inference problem.

The experiments cover sampling a multimodal distribution with a learned annealing path, learning approximations to future-observation likelihoods in a hidden Markov model, and amortized inference in hierarchical deep generative models. Optimizing the nested objectives improves sample quality as measured by log average weight and effective sample size. The results support learning guidance throughout the sampling process, rather than treating intermediate sampling choices as fixed.
neurips-2021-nested-variational-inferenc.tldr: Nested variational inference learns proposals and intermediate distributions at multiple sampling levels, improving reported sample-quality measures.

paragraphs: Graph learning often benefits from smoothing features or predicted labels across connected nodes. The challenge is deciding how far that smoothing should go. Too few iterations may leave useful neighborhood information uncombined, while too many may oversmooth it. Because nodes differ in degree and local structure, a single iteration count may be unsuitable for the whole graph.

Node-dependent local smoothing, or NDLS, assigns each node its own smoothing iteration count. It computes influence scores from the adjacency matrix and chooses the count by applying a threshold to those scores. The selected counts can then control either feature smoothing or label smoothing, making the procedure useful at different stages of prediction.

The authors report state-of-the-art node-classification performance, fast training, and support for large graphs. They also describe the method as compatible with arbitrary models. The central contribution is to make smoothing a locally controlled operation: each node's treatment reflects its graph neighborhood, while the smoothing procedure remains flexible enough to accompany different predictive architectures.
neurips-2021-node-dependent-local-smooth.tldr: NDLS chooses a separate smoothing depth for each graph node using influence scores, with strong reported accuracy and scalability.

paragraphs: This paper analyzes the training and generalization of recurrent neural networks with random initialization. It asks which functions of an input sequence can be learned with provable error guarantees and how the required training iterations and samples grow with sequence length. The results extend earlier guarantees in two distinct ways.

First, the authors analyze the neural tangent kernel matrix to handle functions formed by summing contributions from individual sequence positions. They remove an earlier requirement that every input vector have a very small norm depending on the function's complexity. For some notable function classes, they establish iteration and sample requirements that grow almost-polynomially with sequence length.

Second, the paper covers functions that jointly depend on several selected sequence positions and cannot be written as additive contributions. The almost-polynomial scaling result applies when either the number of involved positions is small or their span within the sequence is small. These conditional guarantees broaden the analyzed capabilities of recurrent networks to include interactions among inputs, while specifying when the stated scaling holds.
neurips-2021-on-the-provable-generalizat.tldr: New RNN generalization guarantees remove a restrictive input-norm condition and cover certain interactions among sequence positions.

paragraphs: Hierarchical clustering creates nested groupings that can be examined at different numbers of clusters. This paper develops a parallel algorithm for the Euclidean hierarchical k-median problem. Its aim is to combine efficient distributed computation with guarantees on the quality of the clustering obtained at different levels of the hierarchy.

For any fixed k, the expected cost is within an O(min{d, log n} log Δ) factor of optimum. Here n counts points, d is dimension, and Δ is the ratio of largest to smallest pairwise distance. A separate guarantee covers all k simultaneously with an additional logarithmic factor. Keeping these statements separate matters because the fixed-k result is explicitly an expectation guarantee.

The algorithm assumes per-machine memory of at least order log²(n + Δ + d), and its round bound decreases as available memory grows. The authors describe it as, to their knowledge, the first parallel hierarchical k-median algorithm with theoretical guarantees. An empirical study also supports its practical effectiveness, complementing the approximation and parallel-computation analysis.
neurips-2021-parallel-and-efficient-hier.tldr: A parallel Euclidean hierarchical k-median algorithm provides approximation and round-complexity guarantees, supported by an empirical study.

paragraphs: Linear-programming applications often require both large problem sizes and highly accurate solutions. This paper presents PDLP, a first-order solver designed to meet those requirements. Its central computations are matrix-vector multiplications, providing a basis for scaling to very large instances while pursuing the accuracy expected in traditional linear programming.

PDLP applies primal-dual hybrid gradient to a saddle-point formulation of the problem. It strengthens that starting point with diagonal preconditioning, presolving, adaptive step sizes, and adaptive restarting. The contribution lies in combining these techniques into a practical solver, rather than relying on the unmodified optimization method alone.

On 383 instances derived from MIPLIB 2017, with a relative-accuracy target of 10⁻⁸ and a one-hour limit, PDLP reduces geometric-mean solve time by a factor of 6.3 relative to SCS. Unsolved instances fall from 227 to 49. The authors also identify benchmark problems and a PageRank application where their open-source Julia prototype outperforms a commercial solver. These results demonstrate high-accuracy first-order solving in the evaluated settings.
neurips-2021-practical-large-scale-linea.tldr: PDLP combines primal-dual hybrid gradient with practical enhancements to solve large linear programs accurately and faster in reported comparisons.

paragraphs: This paper studies what can be recovered from a random bipartite graph whose connections are generated according to a matrix M. The graph is sparse in the sense that entries of M are bounded above by a sparsity parameter. The authors investigate how this sparsity affects estimation of both the matrix and its underlying column space.

These are related but distinct targets. Estimating M seeks to recover the connectivity structure itself. Estimating its column space seeks the subspace represented by its columns, evaluated through the corresponding projection matrix. For both targets, the paper measures error using operator and Frobenius norms, giving two mathematical views of estimation accuracy.

The authors propose estimators and show that they attain minimax-optimal rates. This means their error rates match the best possible worst-case rates for the analyzed problem setting. The result makes sparsity part of the statistical account of recoverability and establishes optimal-rate performance for both direct connectivity estimation and the more structural task of recovering its column space.
neurips-2021-rate-optimal-subspace-estim.tldr: The paper establishes minimax-optimal rates for estimating connectivity matrices and their column spaces in sparse random bipartite graphs.

paragraphs: Many causal-discovery methods rely on faithfulness to guarantee correctness as data grows. Approximate violations of that assumption can lead to poor results. Exact score-based search offers a route to weaker assumptions, but searching over large graphs is computationally difficult. This paper addresses that scalability problem in the linear Gaussian setting.

The authors estimate a super-structure, a graph that restricts the candidate relationships considered during exact search. They construct it from the support of the inverse covariance matrix under assumptions strictly weaker than faithfulness. This narrows the search space using an estimated structure before the more expensive search procedure is applied.

A second strategy performs exact search within local clusters containing each variable and its neighbors up to two hops away in the super-structure. Numerical experiments demonstrate high accuracy and scalability to hundreds of nodes. The contribution combines weaker structural assumptions with ways to organize and restrict computation, making exact score-based techniques more practical in the setting studied without claiming to remove assumptions altogether.
neurips-2021-reliable-causal-discovery-w.tldr: Super-structure estimation and local exact search improve linear Gaussian causal discovery under assumptions weaker than faithfulness.

paragraphs: Understanding a scene as a collection of objects is difficult when the observer's viewpoint is also changing. The image reflects both what is in the scene and where it is viewed from. SIMONe addresses this joint problem by learning representations from RGB video alone through an unsupervised variational approach.

The model separates its latent representation into object and frame components. Object latents capture time-invariant information about individual scene elements, while frame latents capture global changes over time, such as viewpoint. Shared structure across scenes supports this separation. The resulting object descriptions are allocentric: they represent objects independently of the observer's particular view.

The same factorization lets the model separate object dynamics and summarize trajectories as per-object properties across time. The authors demonstrate these capabilities on three procedurally generated video datasets, alongside results for view synthesis and instance segmentation. The significance is that a video can supply both persistent object descriptions and changing frame information within one representation, supporting scene understanding beyond the appearance of any single image.
neurips-2021-simone-view-invariant-tempo.tldr: SIMONe separates video into object and frame latents to learn viewpoint-independent object descriptions and trajectory summaries without supervision.

paragraphs: Pairwise learning uses losses defined on two examples, as in ranking and metric learning. For streaming data, a common approach pairs each new example with a stored buffer of earlier examples. Maintaining a sufficiently large buffer creates memory and computation costs. This paper proposes stochastic and online gradient methods that pair each example only with its immediate predecessor.

That simple update creates a subtle analytical challenge: the current model and the previous example are statistically dependent. The authors introduce techniques to separate this dependency in the analysis. They establish stability results and bounds on optimization and generalization error across convex and nonconvex settings, including smooth and nonsmooth problems.

The results resolve an open question about obtaining meaningful generalization bounds for online gradient descent with a very small fixed buffer. The authors also extend their algorithms and stability analysis to differentially private pairwise learning, reporting significant improvements over existing results. The contribution combines a minimal-storage update rule with theory explaining its learning behavior, rather than requiring a growing collection of past examples.
neurips-2021-simple-stochastic-and-onlin.tldr: Pairing each example only with its predecessor yields efficient pairwise-learning algorithms with new generalization and privacy results.

paragraphs: Differentially private learning often treats each person as contributing one sample. This paper instead lets each user hold multiple samples and protects that user's complete contribution. It investigates how additional samples per person can reduce the number of distinct users needed for private learning, making the unit of privacy central to the analysis.

With sufficiently many samples per user, the authors show that any privately learnable class can be learned under approximate differential privacy using O(log(1/δ)/ε) users. For pure differential privacy, they establish an Oε(d) user bound even in the local model, where d is probabilistic representation dimension. Nearly matching lower bounds show that these user requirements are close to optimal.

The proof machinery extends global stability to allow public randomness. Correlated sampling then raises stability arbitrarily close to one at a polynomial cost in samples. The result therefore describes a conditional trade-off: fewer participating users become sufficient when each contributes enough data, with the stability construction explaining how those additional samples support private learning.
neurips-2021-user-level-differentially-p.tldr: With sufficiently many samples per person, correlated sampling enables user-level private learning with nearly optimal numbers of users.
